Stage 3 · Reading

The shop that fixes things

One evening in Amsterdam in 2009, and what happened to the idea afterwards.

🔧☕
1 · Before you read. Your kettle stops working. What do you actually do?

Choose one and say why. Compare with a partner before you read.Choose one and say why before you read.Choose one and note your reason. You will check it against the text.

The shop that fixes things

Written for this course, from the Repair Café International Foundation’s published account of its own history. The town in paragraphs 3 and 4 is a composite of several such groups.

1The idea did not come up in a laboratory. In 2009 a Dutch journalist called Martine Postma, who had been writing about sustainability and had noticed how much her neighbours were throwing away, came up with something specific: one afternoon, one hall, free coffee, and volunteers who could hold a screwdriver. The first Repair Café was held in Amsterdam on 18 October 2009. She was not sure anybody would turn up. Instead, people arrived early, carrying appliances, clothes, furniture and, in at least one case, a musical instrument.

2What happened next was not planned either. So many groups wanted to do the same thing that a foundation was set up in March 2010 simply to answer them, and it began producing manuals, posters and a starter kit so that nobody had to work out the format from scratch. Consequently, similar shops popped up in one country after another. By 2016 there were more than a thousand registered; today the figure has passed three thousand. Admittedly, that is still small against the scale of what gets discarded — but it grew without advertising, which is unusual.

3In practice, a session looks less impressive than the numbers. In one English town that started a group after a public meeting, nineteen people turned up on the first Saturday, most of them over sixty, and they repaired forty-one things before lunch. Nobody had to make up a reason for coming. A lamp is not a symbol of anything; it is a lamp, and it either works afterwards or it does not.

4The economics are what persuade councils, however, rather than the sentiment. A repair typically costs a fraction of a replacement, and volunteers find out very quickly that a surprising share of dead appliances have one cheap broken part. Nevertheless, nobody pretends the saving is large in itself. Therefore the case for the shop tends to be financial before it is ever environmental. In that town the funding ran out in the second winter, and yet the group stayed open, staffed by eleven volunteers and one paid hour a week.

5The foundation has also tried to sort out a problem the volunteers created themselves. Every session generates knowledge — which brands fail, which faults recur, which parts cannot be bought — and for years all of it stayed in people’s heads. In 2017, therefore, an online tool was launched so that groups could record what each repair turned out to involve. Moreover, the records made it possible to compare one town with another. In other words, a movement built on Saturday afternoons quietly began to carry out research.

6None of which has fixed the underlying problem. Manufacturers still design products that are difficult to open, and several countries are only now beginning to phase out the rules that allowed it. Even so, the interesting part of the story is not the tools or the money. What turned out to matter was that somebody organised an afternoon and other people came. That is the least repeatable part of it, and it is the only part the starter kit cannot explain.

Text A · One afternoon in Amsterdam

Written for this course, from the Repair Café International Foundation’s published account of its own history.

The idea did not come up in a laboratory. In 2009 a Dutch journalist called Martine Postma, who had been writing about sustainability and had noticed how much her neighbours were throwing away, came up with something specific: one afternoon, one hall, free coffee, and volunteers who could hold a screwdriver. The first Repair Café was held in Amsterdam on 18 October 2009. She was not sure anybody would turn up. Instead, people arrived early, carrying appliances, clothes, furniture and, in at least one case, a musical instrument.

What happened next was not planned either. So many groups wanted to do the same thing that a foundation was set up in March 2010 simply to answer them, and it began producing manuals, posters and a starter kit so that nobody had to work out the format from scratch. Consequently, similar shops popped up in one country after another. By 2016 there were more than a thousand registered; today the figure has passed three thousand. Admittedly, that is still small against the scale of what gets discarded — but it grew without advertising, which is unusual.

The foundation has also tried to sort out a problem the volunteers created themselves. Every session generates knowledge — which brands fail, which faults recur, which parts cannot be bought — and for years all of it stayed in people’s heads. In 2017, therefore, an online tool was launched so that groups could record what each repair turned out to involve. Moreover, the records made it possible to compare one town with another. In other words, a movement built on Saturday afternoons quietly began to carry out research.

Text B · What a Saturday actually looks like

Written for this course. The town described here is a composite of several such groups.

In practice, a session looks less impressive than the numbers. In one English town that started a group after a public meeting, nineteen people turned up on the first Saturday, most of them over sixty, and they repaired forty-one things before lunch. Nobody had to make up a reason for coming. A lamp is not a symbol of anything; it is a lamp, and it either works afterwards or it does not.

The economics are what persuade councils, however, rather than the sentiment. A repair typically costs a fraction of a replacement, and volunteers find out very quickly that a surprising share of dead appliances have one cheap broken part. Nevertheless, nobody pretends the saving is large in itself. Therefore the case for the shop tends to be financial before it is ever environmental. In that town the funding ran out in the second winter, and yet the group stayed open, staffed by eleven volunteers and one paid hour a week.

None of which has fixed the underlying problem. Manufacturers still design products that are difficult to open, and several countries are only now beginning to phase out the rules that allowed it. Even so, the interesting part of the story is not the tools or the money. What turned out to matter was that somebody organised an afternoon and other people came. That is the least repeatable part of it, and it is the only part the starter kit cannot explain, which is presumably why the foundation spends so much of its time answering the same question from towns that already have everything else they need.

1 · Read the explanation.
One procedure for both forms

Ask four questions in order. First: is there a preposition immediately in front? If yes, use -ing, whatever else is true. Second: is there a modal (can, could, must, should, will, might)? If yes, use the bare verb with no to. Third: does the gap answer the question why, or does it follow a noun or an adjective? If yes, use to + verb. Fourth: is there a verb in front that has its own pattern? Then use that pattern.

The verb patterns, in short. Always -ing: enjoy, avoid, finish, mind, imagine, suggest, keep, practise, deny, miss. Always to: want, hope, decide, refuse, promise, offer, manage, afford, bother, agree, need, seem. Object then to: ask, tell, remind, advise, allow, expect. Either, with no change: begin, start, continue, like, love, hate, prefer.

The five that change meaning. Remember, forget, stop, try, regret. The -ing form looks back at something that happened; the infinitive looks forward to a task, a purpose or an announcement.

Where neither rule applies. An -ing form can also shorten a relative clause (a website explaining how it works) or attach a reason to the whole sentence (Knowing the funding was gone, they stayed open anyway). In both cases the subject must be the same as the main clause.

Negatives. Not always goes in front of the whole form: decided not to say, fed up with not having enough, hard not to agree.

The commonest errors at this level
  • I suggest to set up a shop instead of suggest setting up.
  • They agreed phasing out the service instead of agreed to phase out.
  • They came here for find out instead of to find out.
  • She can to hold a screwdriver after a modal.
  • To organise it was the hard part where English would say Organising it.

Two things to watch

1 — The preposition rule beats everything. If a preposition is in front, no other question matters.

2 — Suggest and agree are the two most often confused. Suggest doing, agree to do. Learn them as a pair and half the mistakes disappear.

5 · Worked example. Read it before you do the exercises.
Running the four questions

The sentence: They suggested ______ (set up) a website instead of ______ (rely) on the council.

Gap 1 — question 1: is there a preposition in front? No, there is a verb: suggested. Skip to question 4: suggest is on the -ing list. So: setting up.

Gap 2 — question 1: the words in front are instead of, which is a preposition. That settles it immediately: relying. No other question needs asking.

A third gap: They stayed late ______ (finish) the rota. No preposition, no modal, and the gap answers why did they stay late. Question 3 applies: to finish.

The order matters. A learner who starts at question 4 will look for a verb pattern that is not there and guess. A learner who starts at question 1 gets most gaps without thinking at all.

13 · Read this before the extra practice.
One procedure instead of six rules

Look at what stands in front of the gap and work down the list. The first match wins.

1. A preposition? → -ing, always: fed up with waiting, look forward to hearing, without having to ask. 2. A modal? → the bare verb: could hold. 3. Does it answer why? → to + verb: a survey to find out what was thrown away. 4. A noun or adjective in front? → to + verb: nothing to repair, ready to start, too late to apply, It is easy to criticise.

5. Is it standing where a noun would? → -ing: Organising it was the hard part. 6. A verb in front? → that verb’s own pattern, from lesson 33. 7. Shortening a relative clause? → -ing or -ed: a website explaining the model. And whatever the answer, a negative puts not first: decided not to close, without not having… → fed up with not having.

Where the procedure earns its keep

Two places. First, the phrases where to is a preposition, because question 1 catches them before you can mistake them for infinitives: look forward to hearing, be used to working, object to paying. Test it by putting a noun after: if look forward to the weekend works, the to is a preposition.

Second, the verbs from lesson 33 where the form is the meaning. Question 6 sends you to the verb, and the verb decides: They stopped funding it (they ended the funding) against They stopped to fund it (they paused in order to). Same with remember, forget, try. The procedure will not choose the meaning for you; it only tells you that the choice is yours to make here.

One more trap, from lesson 30: a reduced clause of reason needs the same subject as the main clause. Knowing the money was gone, they stayed open works because they knew. Knowing the money was gone, the shop stayed open does not.

Errors to watch: fed up with to wait → waiting · could to hold → could hold · a survey for finding out → to find out · To organise it was the hard part in ordinary English → Organising it was · decided to not close → decided not to close.

1 · Read the model proposal.
Model · a proposal in four paragraphs

The bicycle problem has come up at every residents’ meeting in this building for three years and nothing has been carried out. Sixty flats share a bike store built for twenty, so half the bicycles live in hallways and about a dozen have not moved since 2022. I would suggest starting with one Saturday morning rather than with a building committee.

On that morning we would do two things. First, tag every bicycle in the store and in the hallways with a paper label; anything still labelled six weeks later has an owner who has forgotten it. Second, carry out a two-question survey at the door to find out how many people would use a store if there were room. Moreover, one resident repairs bicycles for a living and has offered an hour, which means anything abandoned but usable could be worked on rather than thrown out.

Admittedly, this does not sort out the underlying problem, which is that the store is too small and nobody is going to build a new one. Even so, twelve dead bicycles removed is twelve spaces, and that is roughly what a new rack would cost thirty thousand tenge to achieve. Consequently the case is worth making at the next meeting even to people who are indifferent to bicycles.

If nobody turns up, we have lost a Saturday. If eleven people turn up, we have a rota. In other words, the thing that decides this is not the labels or the survey but whether one person is willing to organise a morning.
